content: The RTL6 protein, also known as Retrotransposon Gag Like 6, is encoded by the RTL6 gene in humans. This gene belongs to the Mart family, which is related to Sushi-like retrotransposons and is thought to have originated from fish and amphibians. The RTL6 protein is localized in the nucleus and contains a predicted leucine zipper motif, which is known to bind nucleic acids in similar proteins, such as LDOCL1. The gene is also referred to by aliases such as LDOCL1L, MAR6, MART6, and SIRH3. It is composed of two exons and spans 5556 base pairs of DNA. The RTL6 gene is classified as a retrotransposon GAG-related gene and is one of eleven MART (Mammalian Retrotransposon-Derived) genes in humans. These genes are related to Sushi-like retrotransposons with long terminal repeats, which originated from fish and amphibians. Between 170 and 310 million years ago, MART genes lost their ability to retrotranspose and simultaneously acquired new, beneficial functions for their host organisms. The RTL6 mRNA has an alternative transcription start site located 140 base pairs upstream of the normal transcribed region. The primary mRNA transcript is 5355 base pairs long, while the transcript with the upstream start site is 5495 base pairs in length. The primary amino acid sequence of the RTL6 protein consists of 239 residues. No alternative splice variants of the protein have been identified. RTL6 is rich in proline and arginine residues. The protein contains a predicted leucine zipper motif, which is known to facilitate nucleic acid binding in other proteins. Additionally, it has a domain of unknown function spanning amino acid residues 98 to 177. RTL6 is part of the DUF4939 (domain of unknown function) superfamily. The secondary structure of RTL6 is predominantly composed of alpha helices. A specific region of the protein, spanning amino acid residues 29 to 63, is predicted to form a coiled-coil structure. Post-translational modifications of RTL6 include two predicted phosphorylation sites for Protein Kinase C at residues 6 and 45, both with high confidence scores. There is also a predicted ubiquitination site at residue 8, with medium confidence. Based on its structural features, including the leucine zipper domain, and the absence of signals for secretion or transmembrane domains, RTL6 is expected to localize to the nucleus and cytosol. Immunohistochemical staining supports this localization. RTL6 is expressed at high levels during all stages of development and across a wide variety of tissues. Its expression decreases in HeLa cervical cancer cells following treatment with chemotherapeutic agents such as Casiopeinas and in A549 lung cancer cells after treatment with Actinomycin D. The RTL6 protein has been shown to interact with the UXAC protein from Yersinia pestis, the gram-negative bacterium responsible for the bubonic plague. In terms of homology and evolution, RTL6 has eleven paralogs in humans, which exhibit diverse functions and expression patterns. Many of these paralogs contain zinc finger domains and are known to bind nucleic acids. RTL6 is highly conserved across mammals, including its leucine zipper motif and DUF4939 domain. The gene is also conserved in marsupials, such as the opossum, but not in birds, such as the chicken. This suggests that RTL6 likely originated after the divergence of mammals and birds but before the divergence of marsupials and placental mammals, approximately 170 to 310 million years ago. The most distantly related organisms with homologous genes are bony fishes, such as salmon and common carp, although their protein sequences show significantly less similarity to the human RTL6 protein compared to mammals.
